title: Grade 8 Science — Mon, Jun 23
description: Force and Pressure — Day 1 of 5: Force — types, effects, contact vs non-contact
subject: science

questions.question: Force is defined as:
options: A push or pull on an object — can change its speed, direction, shape, or state of rest/motion
The momentum of a moving object
questions.explanation: Force = a push or pull. Effects: (1) set a stationary object in motion, (2) stop a moving object, (3) change speed, (4) change direction, (5) change shape. SI unit = Newton (N). Force is a vector — it has both magnitude and direction.

questions.question: Contact forces require physical contact between objects. Which of these is a CONTACT force?
questions.explanation: Contact forces require touching: friction, normal reaction, tension, applied force, muscular force. Non-contact (action at a distance): gravity, magnetic force, electrostatic force. Friction is the classic contact force — two surfaces must touch for friction to act.

questions.question: A magnet attracting an iron nail without touching it is an example of:
questions.explanation: Non-contact force: acts without physical contact, across a distance. Examples: gravity (Earth pulls Moon without touching), magnetic force (magnet attracts iron), electrostatic force (charged comb attracts paper). The iron nail is attracted through air — no contact needed.

questions.question: When two forces act on an object in the SAME direction, the net force is:
questions.explanation: Forces in same direction: net force = F₁ + F₂ (add). Forces in opposite directions: net force = |F₁ − F₂| (subtract). If equal and opposite: net force = 0 (object stays still or moves at constant speed — balanced forces). This is Newton's first law in action.

questions.question: Two children push a box from opposite sides with forces 30 N and 20 N. The net force and direction =
questions.explanation: Opposite directions: net force = 30−20 = 10 N. Direction = toward the greater force (30 N side). The box moves toward the child pushing with 30 N. If both pushed with 30 N: net = 0, box wouldn't move.

questions.question: Gravity is a non-contact force. What keeps the Moon in orbit around Earth?
options: Gravitational force — Earth pulls the Moon without contact, providing centripetal force for circular orbit
questions.explanation: Gravity acts across 3.84 lakh km of space between Earth and Moon. This gravitational pull provides the centripetal force that keeps the Moon in orbit. No contact, no physical link — pure non-contact force. Newton observed this connection between falling apple and orbiting Moon.

questions.question: Muscular force is a type of:
options: Contact force — muscles must be attached to or in contact with an object to exert force
questions.explanation: Muscular force = force exerted by muscles. Always requires contact: your hand touching a ball, your foot kicking a door. Animals use muscular force for all voluntary movement. Even when animals lift heavy loads — muscles contract and pull bones (levers) in contact with the load.

questions.question: A force can change the SHAPE of an object. Which example demonstrates this?
options: Kicking a football to make it move
Squeezing a rubber ball — it flattens
A magnet rotating a compass needle
questions.explanation: Effects of force: (1) motion, (2) stop motion, (3) change direction, (4) change shape. Squeezing a rubber ball changes its shape (deformation). Kicking = motion change. Gravity = direction of motion change. Compass = rotation/direction. Only squeezing changes shape.

questions.question: Electrostatic force is a non-contact force. When a plastic comb rubbed on hair attracts small bits of paper, this is because:
options: The comb gains electric charge through friction; the charged comb exerts electrostatic force on neutral paper at a distance
The paper has iron in it
Gravity becomes stronger near the comb
questions.explanation: Rubbing = friction between comb and hair → comb gains static electric charge (becomes charged). Charged comb exerts electrostatic force on uncharged paper (induces opposite charges) → paper is attracted. Non-contact: comb doesn't touch paper initially. This is electrostatics (static electricity).

questions.question: Forces are BALANCED when:
options: The object is always at rest
Net force = 0 — equal forces act in opposite directions; object remains at rest OR moves at constant speed
questions.explanation: Balanced forces: net force = 0. Result: no change in motion state (stays still or stays at constant velocity). Unbalanced forces: net force ≠ 0 → object accelerates (speeds up, slows down, or changes direction). A book on a table: weight down, normal force up — balanced → book stays still.

questions.question: The SI unit of force is:
questions.explanation: Force SI unit = Newton (N), named after Isaac Newton. 1 N = force needed to accelerate 1 kg mass by 1 m/s². Derived unit: 1 N = 1 kg⋅m/s². Common forces: gravitational force on 1 kg ≈ 10 N (g ≈ 10 m/s²).

questions.question: A ball rolling on the ground eventually stops. The force responsible for this is:
options: Friction between ball and ground — a contact force opposing motion
questions.explanation: Rolling friction (a type of friction) between ball and ground opposes the ball's motion and gradually slows it to a stop. Gravity acts perpendicular to motion (downward), so it doesn't stop the ball. Without friction (e.g., in space), the ball would roll forever (Newton's 1st law).

questions.question: Two tug-of-war teams pull a rope: Team A pulls with 500 N, Team B with 500 N in opposite direction. What happens?
options: Net force = 0 — forces are balanced — rope does not move (draw)
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite forces = balanced = zero net force = no acceleration = no movement. This is Newton's 1st law: balanced forces → no change in state. In reality, tug-of-war is won when one team applies more force, making forces unbalanced.

questions.question: Can a force change the direction of motion without changing speed?
options: Yes — for example, a satellite in circular orbit: gravity changes direction continuously but speed stays constant (in ideal circular orbit)
Only magnetic forces can change direction
questions.explanation: Force can change direction without changing speed. Circular motion example: Earth's gravity provides centripetal force on a satellite — constantly changing direction toward Earth's centre, but for a circular orbit, speed remains constant. Roller coaster turns: force changes direction not speed.

questions.question: Which pair correctly classifies the forces?
questions.explanation: Correct: Friction (surfaces must touch) = contact. Gravity (acts across any distance, no contact needed) = non-contact. Common confusion: normal force and tension are also contact forces. Magnetic, electrostatic, gravitational are non-contact (action at a distance).
